title: Lifetime and pointer errors
goal: Copy a value while its temporary object is alive and send the result into a live object owned by the caller.

prerequisites.text: You need a block in braces, addresses, dereferencing and output parameters.

terms.title: Object lifetime
terms.definition: The period during execution when an object exists. The local sensor in the inner block ends its lifetime when execution leaves that block.

terms.title: Dangling pointer
terms.definition: A common name for a pointer whose original object no longer exists. Access through such a pointer is invalid.

terms.title: Output parameter
terms.definition: A pointer to a live caller-owned object where the function writes a result on success.

sections.title: Keep the number after the reading ends
paragraphs: An inner block gets a reading. Later code needs that number. Copy the reading into an outer variable while the source object is still alive.

An address and a copied value have different periods of use. A pointer to a local object in the inner block is usable for access only during the object’s lifetime. The copied integer remains usable as long as saved lives.
A function can use the same model with an int *out from its caller. During the call, &sample points to a live object. The function copies the number there after a successful read.

Mark entry to the inner block, result storage and the end of the block on a timeline. The temporary sensor's address is useful while the object exists. If the number is needed later, copy the number itself into a variable created outside the block. The result then has a lifetime of its own.

sections.title: The integer 9 outlives the inner block
paragraphs: The object on the left of the assignment belongs to the outer block. On the right, the code reads sensor while execution is still in its block.
Apply the model to two objects in the reader function. A local number is needed for validation. The caller's object holds the result. The contract connects them by a single copy after success.
steps: main declares saved in the outer block. The inner block creates sensor holding 9.
current receives the address of sensor, which is valid in this block. saved = *current writes 9 into the outer object.
The inner block ends. printf reads only saved, whose lifetime continues.
trace: sensor has yet to be created
sensor and current have ended their lifetimes

sections.title: The address of a local object expires on return
paragraphs: The diagnostic fragment return &local obtains the address of an object inside the function. Its lifetime ends when the function returns. Clang detects the returned address. The displayed diagnostic setting makes the warning a compilation error. Use this fragment to read the compiler diagnostic only.

Establish lifetime from the contract and where the object is created. Once the object reaches the end of its lifetime, stop using the old pointer value, including comparisons with NULL. In the exercise, check out and the read result before writing.

sections.title: Keep the old reading on failure
paragraphs: Suppose the stored reading is -8. Predict what remains after the malformed input -9x, then the result after a valid -9. Point out where the function performs its only write through out.

selfcheck.prompt: read_sample(&sample) gets input 27x and sample began at 17. Why should the output be invalid, and what stays in sample?
selfcheck.feedback: The reader reports a failure. The function rejects it before writing through out, so sample still holds 17.

practice.title: Send a reading to the caller
practice.task: Read an integer from -99 to 99 from the first line. read_sample takes the address of a live caller-owned int, checks it for NULL, reads into a separate local integer, and copies the value into *out only after success. Return 1 after writing and 0 on failure. Print the number on success. On failure, check that the previous value is still 17 and print invalid. The supplied main uses invalid changed to flag a broken contract. Ignore subsequent lines.
practice.hint: On success, copy the local temporary into *out before returning. Keep every failure path ahead of that write.
criteria: Input 27 gives 27, including without a final newline.
Malformed input leaves 17 and gives invalid.
NULL returns 0 before reading or writing through the pointer.

steps.action: Open Practice with input 27. Select Run my code.
steps.why: Match the output with the reading and explain the role of temporary.
steps.expected: The starter prints 17. The specification requires 27.

steps.action: Copy temporary into *out after the successful check and rerun the input.
steps.why: Write the integer into a live caller-owned object before returning.
Check that both failures preserve the previous value.
steps.expected: Both runs give invalid. The invalid changed marker stays absent.

exercises.title: Independent transfer
exercises.task: Save a copy of your corrected main.c in a separate text file. Change INITIAL_SAMPLE to -8, then try -9x and -9 separately. Explain why the failure check compares with the old value. Restore your saved version afterward.
criteria: The first run prints invalid and keeps -8. The second prints -9.
The code keeps no address of temporary and uses none after the function returns.

teaching.scene: A reading is taken in a temporary block and printed later. Identify the integer to keep and the object that is live after the closing brace.

predict.prompt: sensor is 9 in the inner block and current receives its address. What value is available at printf, and which object does the call read?
predict.answer: While the block is active, *current yields 9 and the assignment stores it in saved. After the closing brace, printf reads the live saved object and prints 9.

apply.prompt: Two calls reuse one output variable, which initially holds 17. The first input is 12 and the second is 8x. What is stored after each call, and how many assignments through out happened?
apply.answer: The first call stores 12. The second input is rejected, so the variable still holds 12. There is one write through out, in the successful first call.

practice.strategy: Draw the boundary between parsing and storing the result. Take a valid number and the same number with a suffix. Predict which record leaves the output value as it was.
practice.diagnosis: If main signals changed after a rejection, look for a copy before validation finished. At which step did the program know the whole input was valid?

syntax.explanation: The outer saved object holds a copy of the integer. sensor ends its lifetime earlier, so an address held past that boundary cannot replace the copied value.
syntax.mistake: Returning &local carries the address of an object whose lifetime ends at the return. Use the compile diagnostic to examine this case without executing undefined behavior.
